This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
We are just over a week out from the midterm elections.
The University of Florida election lab, which tracks voting by mail and in person,
says so far more than 30 million Americans have cast their ballots early.
Since last year, President Trump and his allies have put pressure on GOP-led states to redraw
congressional districts to favor Republicans and avoid the historical pattern of heavy midterm
losses for the President's party. Yet as NPR's Samra Keith reports, Republicans are spending
millions on tightly competitive races for House seats that were expected to be easy wins.
Some of these lines were drawn based on the Trump 2024 electorate, which was a real high watermark.
Since then, key pieces of the Trump base have soured on the President, including young voters
and Latino voters. The President's approval rating is now at a new low. A number of Democratic
incumbents who were directly targeted in the new maps decided to stick it out and fight.
NPR's Tamra Keith. Tens of thousands of people are taking flights to Israel to vote in tomorrow's
elections. Polls show an extremely tight race that threatens Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin
Netanyahu's hold on power. NPR's Ruth Sherlock reports from Bangorian Airport in Israel.
People are arriving from all over the world into Bangorian Airport to vote in tomorrow's
elections. An election that Israelis say is pivotal to the future of their country.
Do they want to continue with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the wars that he
is leading across the region? Or is it time for change for a softer, more diplomatic approach?
This is the decision that people have to make tomorrow. There are no mail-in ballots allowed
in this election, so people are coming in person to cast their vote, often spending thousands of
dollars to fly here. NPR's Ruth Sherlock. The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic,
maker of Claude AI, has filed paperwork for an initial public offering. Analysts expect
the listing to be one of the biggest on record. NPR's John Ruitch with more.
Anthropic got its start just five years ago when a group of senior researchers at OpenAI led by
Dario Amade broke away. They were concerned that the company was not on a path to develop AI safely.
Anthropic has since become a juggernaut and OpenAI's biggest competitor was some of the most widely
used AI models on the market. Amade, now CEO, has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings
about the possibility of AI spiraling out of human control. The IPO perspective showed
skyrocketing growth at the company, and analysts say the IPO could value the firm at $1.5 to $2
trillion. John Ruitch, NPR News. U.S. stocks end the day higher with the NASDAQ closing up 214
points. This is NPR News. Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts for the first time
to staff working in the United States, Canada, India, and the United Kingdom at a time when AI
is rapidly evolving. The tech giant announced its plans in a blog post shared with personnel today.
Bloomberg and other news organizations cite a company's spokesperson or memo in reporting
roughly 60,000 people are eligible for the voluntary buyout. The U.S. has not had enough
special education teachers for half a century, and that shortage is getting worse. To help answer
why, NPR's Anaki Mehta has been following over a dozen of those teachers from across the country.
Since the start of the school year, special educators from districts big and small have
been sending us voice memos about their jobs and their lives. "I have a lot of emotions right now."
Teachers like Curie Anderson Walker, Emily Ellis, and Dana Lynn Garcia have been sending us
dispatches as they clean up their classrooms from their drives home. "I had to go to the bathroom
and just cry because I just felt like I failed." "I feel like I was coming into this school year
more prepared this time around." "Yet I feel like the needs are even greater than the year before."
For the rest of the school year, NPR will stay in touch with these educators and go
inside their classrooms to try and understand why these teachers are so hard to find and keep.
Janaki Mehta and PR News. The federal trade commission's suing dollar general, the FTC
accuses the bargain retailer of scamming customers by allegedly charging them more once they reach
the checkout than what was listed on the shelf and in ads. This is NPR News.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks? Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now,
sponsor free through Amazon Music. Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism
and get NPR+ at plus dot npr dot org. That's plus dot npr dot org.

topics.text: Midterm elections approach with over 30 million early votes cast, per University of Florida election lab
Republicans spend millions defending House seats once expected to be easy wins after redistricting
Tens of thousands of Israelis fly home to vote in tight election threatening Netanyahu's hold on power
Anthropic files paperwork for initial public offering, possibly valuing AI firm at $1.5 to $2 trillion
U.S. stocks close higher, with the NASDAQ up 214 points
Microsoft offers first-ever voluntary buyouts to staff in U.S., Canada, India, and United Kingdom
NPR follows special education teachers amid long-running U.S. shortage of special educators
FTC sues Dollar General, accusing it of charging customers more at checkout than listed prices
